355: We find it difficult to express the emotions that agitated Charlotte's soul during all this time, whether toward her husband or toward her unfortunate friend.
Though from what we know of her character we can understand their nature well enough.
356: It is certain that she had resolved to keep Werther at a distance by every means in her power.

And if she hesitated in that decision, it was out of a sincere and friendly pity, knowing how much it would cost him — knowing indeed that he would find it almost impossible to comply with her wishes.
But various causes now urged her to be firm.
Her husband kept a strict silence about the whole matter; and she never made it a subject of conversation, feeling bound to prove to him by her conduct that her feelings agreed with his.
357: That same day — it was the Sunday before Christmas — after Werther had written the letter to his friend just quoted, he came in the evening to Charlotte's house and found her alone.
She was busy preparing some little gifts for her brothers and sisters, to be given out on Christmas Day.

He began talking of the delight of the children, and of that age when the sudden appearance of the Christmas tree, hung with fruit and sweets and lit with wax candles, brings on such transports of joy.
"You shall have a gift too, if you behave well," said Charlotte, hiding her embarrassment behind a sweet smile.
"And what do you call behaving well?"
"What should I do, what can I do, my dear Charlotte?" he said.
"Thursday night," she answered, "is Christmas Eve."
"The children are all to be here, and my father too; there is a present for each of them. Come then as well — but do not come before."
Werther started.
"I want you not to," she went on. "It must be so."
"I ask it of you as a favour, for my own peace and quiet."
"We cannot go on like this any longer."
He turned his face away and walked hastily up and down the room, muttering indistinctly, "We cannot go on like this any longer!"
Charlotte, seeing the violent agitation these words had thrown him into, tried to turn his thoughts with other questions, but in vain.
"No, Charlotte!" he exclaimed. "I will never see you again!"
"And why not?" she answered.
"We may — we must see each other again; only let it be with more discretion."
"Oh, why were you born with that excessive, that ungovernable passion for everything dear to you?"
Then, taking his hand, she said, "I beg you to be calmer. Your talents, your understanding, your genius will give you a thousand resources."
"Be a man, and conquer an unhappy attachment to a creature who can do nothing but pity you."
He bit his lips and looked at her with a gloomy face.
She went on holding his hand.
"Grant me a moment's patience, Werther," she said.
"Do you not see that you are deceiving yourself, that you are seeking your own destruction?"
"Why must you love me — me only, who belong to another?"
"I fear, I greatly fear, that it is only the impossibility of possessing me that makes your desire for me so strong."
He drew his hand back, looking at her with a wild and angry expression.
"That is well!" he exclaimed. "That is very well!"
"Did Albert not furnish you with that reflection?"
"It is profound — a very profound remark."
"A reflection anyone might easily make," she answered. "And is there not one woman in the whole world who is free, and has it in her power to make you happy?"
"Conquer yourself: look for such a woman, and believe me when I say you will certainly find her."
"I have long felt for you, and for all of us: you have shut yourself up too long inside too narrow a circle."
"Conquer yourself; make an effort. A short journey will do you good."
"Seek out an object worthy of your love, and find it; then come back here, and let us enjoy together all the happiness of the most perfect friendship."
358: "This speech," replied Werther with a cold smile, "this speech should be printed, for the benefit of all teachers."
"My dear Charlotte, allow me only a little time longer, and all will be well."
"But all the same, Werther," she added, "do not come again before Christmas."
He was about to answer when Albert came in.
They greeted each other coldly, and paced up and down the room in mutual embarrassment.
Werther made some commonplace remarks; Albert did the same, and their conversation soon dropped.
Albert asked his wife about some household matters; and finding that his errands had not been done, he used expressions that sounded to Werther extremely harsh.
He wanted to go, but had no power to move; and so he stayed until eight o'clock, his uneasiness and discontent steadily increasing.
At length the cloth was laid for supper, and he took up his hat and stick.
Albert invited him to stay; but Werther, fancying it was only a formal compliment, thanked him coldly and left the house.
359: Werther came home, took the candle from his servant, and went up to his room alone.
For some time he talked to himself with great earnestness, wept aloud, and walked about his chamber in great agitation.
At length, without undressing, he threw himself on the bed, where his servant found him at eleven o'clock, when he ventured in to take off his boots.
Werther did not stop him, but forbade him to come in the morning until he should ring.
360: On Monday morning, the twenty-first of December, he wrote Charlotte the following letter, which was found sealed on his desk after his death and given to her.
I shall set it down in fragments, since from several signs it appears to have been written that way.
361: "It is all over, Charlotte: I am resolved to die!"
"I make this declaration deliberately and coolly, with no romantic passion in it, on the morning of the day when I am to see you for the last time."

"By the time you read these lines, O best of women, the cold grave will hold the lifeless remains of that restless and unhappy creature who, in the last moments of his life, knew no pleasure so great as talking with you."
"I have passed a dreadful night — or rather, let me say, a fortunate one; for it has given me resolution, it has fixed my purpose."
"I am resolved to die."

"When I tore myself away from you yesterday, my senses were in tumult and disorder; my heart was oppressed, hope and pleasure had fled from me for ever, and a petrifying cold had seized my wretched being."
"I could scarcely reach my room."
"I threw myself on my knees; and Heaven, for the last time, granted me the consolation of tears."
"A thousand ideas, a thousand schemes rose in my soul, until at last one final, fixed thought took possession of my heart."
"It was to die."
"I lay down to rest; and in the morning, in the quiet hour of waking, the same determination was on me."
"To die!"
"It is not despair: it is the conviction that I have filled up the measure of my sufferings, that I have reached my appointed term, and must sacrifice myself for you."
"Yes, Charlotte, why should I not admit it?"
"One of us three must die: let it be Werther."
"O beloved Charlotte, this heart, whipped up by rage and fury, has often conceived the horrid idea of murdering your husband — you — myself!"
"The lot is cast at last."
"And in the bright, quiet evenings of summer, when you sometimes walk toward the mountains, let your thoughts turn to me."

"Remember how often you have watched me coming up out of the valley to meet you; then turn your eyes to the churchyard that holds my grave, and by the light of the setting sun see how the evening breeze waves the tall grass above my tomb."
"I was calm when I began this letter, but the memory of these scenes makes me weep like a child."
362: About ten in the morning Werther called his servant, and while he was dressing told him that in a few days he meant to set out on a journey.

He therefore told him to lay his clothes in order and get them ready for packing, to call in all his accounts, to fetch home the books he had lent out, and to give two months' pay to the poor dependants who used to receive a weekly allowance from him.
363: He breakfasted in his room, and then mounted his horse and went to visit the steward, who was not at home.
He walked thoughtfully in the garden, and seemed anxious to go over again every idea that was most painful to him.
364: The children did not let him stay alone for long.
They followed him, skipping and dancing in front of him, and told him that after tomorrow, and tomorrow, and one day more, they would get their Christmas present from Charlotte.
And then they recounted all the wonders their child imaginations had built up.
"Tomorrow and tomorrow," he said, "and one day more!"
He was going, but the younger boy stopped him to whisper something in his ear.
He told him that his elder brothers had written splendid New Year's wishes — so large! — one for papa, and another for Albert and Charlotte, and one for Werther.
They were to be presented early in the morning on New Year's Day.
He made each of the children a present, mounted his horse, left his compliments for papa and mamma, and rode away from the place with tears in his eyes.
365: He came home about five o'clock, told his servant to keep the fire up, asked him to pack his books and linen at the bottom of the trunk and put his coats on top.
He then appears to have added the following to the letter addressed to Charlotte.
366: "You think I will obey you, and not visit you again until Christmas Eve."
"On Christmas Eve you will hold this paper in your hand; you will tremble, and wet it with your tears."
"Oh, how happy I feel now that I am determined!"
367: Charlotte, meanwhile, was in a pitiable state of mind.
After her last conversation with Werther she found how painful it would be to refuse his visits, and knew how badly he would suffer from their separation.
368: She had mentioned casually to Albert that Werther would not come back before Christmas Eve.
Soon afterwards Albert rode off to see a man in the neighbourhood, on business that would keep him away all night.
369: None of her family were near her, and she gave herself up to the thoughts that quietly took possession of her mind.
She was united for ever to a husband whose love and fidelity she had proved, to whom she was heartily devoted, and who seemed a special gift from Heaven to secure her happiness.
On the other hand, Werther had become dear to her.
There had been a warm unanimity of feeling between them from the very first hour of their acquaintance, and their long association and repeated meetings had made an indelible impression on her heart.
She had grown used to sharing with him every thought and feeling that interested her, and his absence threatened to open a void in her life that might be impossible to fill.
How heartily she wished she could turn him into a brother, or persuade him to marry one of her own friends, or re-establish his old intimacy with Albert.
370: She passed all her close friends in review before her mind, but found something objectionable in each, and could settle on none she would be willing to give him to.
371: Through all these considerations she felt deeply, though indistinctly, that her own real but unspoken wish was to keep him for herself.
And her pure and amiable heart felt an oppression at that thought which seemed to shut out any prospect of happiness.
She was wretched: a dark cloud had come over her mind.
372: It was now half-past six, and she heard Werther's step on the stairs.
She knew his voice at once, asking whether she was at home.
Her heart beat audibly — we could almost say for the first time — at his coming.
It was too late to deny herself; and as he came in she exclaimed, with a kind of ill-concealed confusion, "You have not kept your word!"
"But you should have done as I asked, at least for my sake," she went on.
"I implore you, for both our sakes."
373: She scarcely knew what she was saying or doing, and sent for some friends whose presence might keep her from being left alone with Werther.
He put down some books he had brought, then asked about some others, until she began to hope her friends would arrive soon — while at the same time wishing they would stay away.
374: At one moment she wanted the servant to stay in the next room; then she changed her mind.
Werther meanwhile walked impatiently up and down.
She went to the piano, and resolved not to withdraw.
Then she collected herself and sat down quietly at Werther's side, where he had taken his usual place on the sofa.
375: "Have you brought nothing to read?" she asked.
"There in my drawer," she went on, "you will find your own translation of some of the songs of Ossian."
"I have not read them yet, as I kept hoping to hear you recite them; but for some time now there has been no chance of it."
He smiled, and went for the manuscript, which he took up with a shudder.
He sat down, and with his eyes full of tears, he began to read.
